text: Platform Fundamentals taught you table extension on the task table, where Incident, Problem, and Change each inherit a shared set of fields. The CMDB uses that exact same mechanism on a different base table: cmdb_ci. This lesson walks the real hierarchy built on top of it.

cmdb_ci sits at the top, holding fields every single CI needs regardless of type: name, sys_class_name, operational_status, install_status, support_group, and location, among others. Every subclass you're about to see inherits all of these automatically, with the same names and the same behavior, every time.

On top of that base sit the real subclasses. cmdb_ci_server adds CPU count, RAM, disk capacity, operating system, and virtualization type. cmdb_ci_appl adds version, vendor, and business criticality. cmdb_ci_network_gear adds port count and firmware version. cmdb_ci_database adds database type, schema, and instance name. And cmdb_ci_service, representing business and technical services, gets only a preview here — full depth comes once Chapter 3 introduces CSDM.

A shared base table solves two real problems at once. First, nothing has to reinvent the same dozen common fields from scratch, with no guarantee two developers spelled operational_status the same way. Second, a relationship or a report can reference, quote, any CI, unquote, generically, without knowing or caring which specific subclass a given record belongs to. And just as importantly, CPU and RAM stay where they belong, on cmdb_ci_server, instead of sitting empty and unused on every switch, database, and service.

You now know the real shape of the CI hierarchy and why it exists: shared fields on the base table, specific attributes only where they're actually needed. Next, an honest look at why keeping all of this accurate in a real organization is a genuinely hard, well-documented challenge — not a problem the platform solves for you automatically.
